name: Color Temperature
statement: Light's colour is rated in kelvins, where, oddly, low numbers are warm and high numbers cool.
statementAccent: low numbers are warm and high numbers cool
meaning: Color temperature is a way of describing the colour, or appearance, of light from a source, expressed in kelvins and defined by comparison with the light emitted by an idealized black-body radiator heated to that temperature. As a black body is heated, it glows first red, then orange, yellow, white, and bluish-white at higher temperatures, so the colour of a light source can be matched to the temperature of a black body producing the same colour. The scale is famously counterintuitive: lower colour temperatures, around 2700 to 3000 kelvins, are called warm and look reddish or yellowish, like candlelight and incandescent bulbs, while higher colour temperatures, around 5000 to 6500 kelvins and above, are called cool and look bluish or white, like daylight and overcast sky, which is the reverse of the everyday sense of warm and cool. Candle flame is around 1900 kelvins, incandescent bulbs around 2700 to 3200, daylight around 5500, and clear blue sky much higher still. Color temperature is central to photography, lighting design, and choosing bulbs and displays.
mechanism: Color temperature rests on the physics of black-body, or thermal, radiation. A perfect black body emits light whose colour depends only on its temperature, glowing dull red when moderately hot and shifting through orange, yellow, white, and blue-white as it gets hotter, exactly as heated metal does. The colour of any light source can therefore be characterized by the temperature of the black body that would glow the same colour, its colour temperature in kelvins. Lower temperatures give the reddish light of candles and incandescent bulbs, higher temperatures the bluish-white light of daylight. The warm and cool labels are aesthetic conventions attached to the reddish and bluish ends, opposite to the physics in that hotter black bodies emit bluer, cooler-looking light. For real sources that do not lie exactly on the black-body curve, such as fluorescent lamps and LEDs, a related measure, correlated colour temperature, gives the temperature of the black body whose colour most closely resembles the source. Reference values follow the black-body progression: candle flame low, incandescent around 2700, daylight around 5500 to 6500, and blue sky very high.

examples.text: A warm white bulb around 2700 kelvins glows reddish like incandescent light, while a cool white or daylight bulb around 5000 to 6500 looks bluish.
Candle flame is around 1900 kelvins, incandescent bulbs around 2700, daylight around 5500, and clear blue sky many thousands of kelvins higher.
Photographers set white balance to the light's colour temperature so whites look neutral rather than orange under lamps or blue in shade.

variants.name: Correlated colour temperature
variants.text: The nearest black-body temperature used to describe sources like fluorescent lamps and LEDs that do not lie exactly on the black-body curve.

variants.name: The warm-cool reversal
variants.text: The convention that low colour temperatures are called warm and high ones cool, opposite to the black-body physics in which hotter is bluer.

whyItMatters: Color temperature is a practically important and widely used concept across photography, film, lighting, and display technology. In photography and cinematography it governs white balance, the adjustment that makes whites look neutral rather than tinted orange under lamplight or blue in shade, and it must be matched to the light source or corrected for a natural result. In lighting design and everyday bulb choice, colour temperature distinguishes warm, cosy light from cool, energizing light, guiding the selection of bulbs for homes, offices, and public spaces, with warm white and cool white or daylight labels reflecting the kelvin value. Displays and monitors are set to a standard white point, commonly around 6500 kelvins, for consistent colour. Understanding colour temperature also illuminates the physics of thermal radiation and why the warm-cool labels run opposite to temperature.

working.text: compare a light source's colour to the light a black body would emit at some temperature.
assign the colour temperature in kelvins, low for warm reddish light and high for cool bluish light.
use the value to set white balance, choose bulbs, or calibrate displays, correcting for the light's colour.

limits: Color temperature strictly describes light whose colour lies on the black-body curve; for real sources like fluorescent lamps and LEDs that fall off the curve, only the correlated colour temperature applies, giving the nearest black-body colour, and two sources with the same correlated colour temperature can still render colours differently. The reference values are approximate and vary between and within sources, so figures like 2700 kelvins for a bulb or 6500 for daylight are representative rather than exact. The warm and cool labels are aesthetic conventions opposite to the physics, which can confuse. Colour temperature captures the overall colour of light but not its full spectrum, so it does not by itself describe how accurately a light renders colours, a separate property.
misreadings: Color temperature is counterintuitive: low kelvin values are warm and reddish while high values are cool and bluish, the reverse of the everyday sense, so hotter black bodies actually emit cooler-looking blue light. It is not an exact fixed figure for a given source, since reference values are approximate. And it describes the colour of light, not how faithfully the light renders other colours, which is a separate property, so treating high kelvins as warm, the values as precise constants, or colour temperature as a measure of colour accuracy, misreads a black-body-based description of the colour of light.
origin: A concept from the physics of black-body radiation used across photography and lighting: the colour of a light source described by the temperature in kelvins of a black body glowing the same colour.
